concepts.title: Canvas Area of a Cylindrical-Conical Tent

questions.q: Using the method 'Canvas Area of a Cylindrical-Conical Tent', work with: h = 12, l = 40, r = 400. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of canvas_area.
questions.a: 80384 sq units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Canvas Area of a Cylindrical-Conical Tent' and work with: h = 60, l = 8, r = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of canvas_area.
questions.a: 2009.6 sq units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Canvas Area of a Cylindrical-Conical Tent' refers to.
questions.a: A tent made of a cylinder topped by a cone needs canvas equal to the curved surface of both parts: pi times radius times slant height for the cone, plus 2 pi times radius times height for the cylinder.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Canvas Area of a Cylindrical-Conical Tent'.
questions.a: Splitting the tent bill into small functions such as cyl(h,r) and con(l,r) keeps each area formula in one reusable place.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Canvas Area of a Cylindrical-Conical Tent', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: canvas_area = 3.14 * r * l + 2 * 3.14 * r * h

questions.q: Using the method 'Post-Tax Net Price Function', work with: cost = 50000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of net_price.
questions.a: 59000 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Post-Tax Net Price Function' and work with: cost = 120000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of net_price.
questions.a: 141600 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Post-Tax Net Price Function' refers to.
questions.a: The payable amount for the tent adds 18 percent tax to the canvas cost; wrapping this in a function post_tax_price(cost) lets any product reuse the same tax step.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Post-Tax Net Price Function'.
questions.a: A tax of 18 percent multiplies the cost by 0.18, and the customer pays cost plus that tax.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Post-Tax Net Price Function', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: net_price = cost + 0.18 * cost

concepts.title: The pow Function with a Modulus Argument

questions.q: Evaluate divmod(7, 2) and name the two parts of its result.. Use the method 'The pow Function with a Modulus Argument'. Work with: base = 24, exponent = 10, modulus = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of reduced.
questions.a: 96 units

questions.q: Compute abs(-5.7) and max(23, 4, 56).. Use the method 'The pow Function with a Modulus Argument'. Work with: base = 3, exponent = 4, modulus = 20. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of reduced.
questions.a: 1 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The pow Function with a Modulus Argument' refers to.
questions.a: The built-in pow(x, y) raises x to the power y, and a third argument makes it return the remainder of that power on division by the modulus; other built-ins such as abs, max, min, sum and len inspect or aggregate values.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The pow Function with a Modulus Argument'.
questions.a: pow(5, 2, 4) first squares 5 to get 25, then keeps only the remainder on division by 4.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'The pow Function with a Modulus Argument', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: pow(x, y, z) = x ** y % z

concepts.title: Mean of Floating Values in a List

questions.q: Using the method 'Mean of Floating Values in a List', work with: v1 = 3, v2 = 6, v3 = 80, v4 = 20. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mean.
questions.a: 27.25 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Mean of Floating Values in a List' and work with: v1 = 100, v2 = 500, v3 = 10, v4 = 24. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mean.
questions.a: 158.5 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Mean of Floating Values in a List' refers to.
questions.a: A user defined function can walk a list with a for loop, folding every element into a running total while counting the elements, and the mean is the total divided by that count.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Mean of Floating Values in a List'.
questions.a: The loop does two jobs at once: accumulating the sum and counting how many values entered it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Mean of Floating Values in a List', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: mean = total / count

concepts.title: Mixed Fraction from an Improper Fraction

questions.q: Using the method 'Mixed Fraction from an Improper Fraction', work with: deno = 30, num = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mixed_value.
questions.a: 6.6667 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Mixed Fraction from an Improper Fraction' and work with: deno = 3, num = 120. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mixed_value.
questions.a: 40 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Mixed Fraction from an Improper Fraction' refers to.
questions.a: The function mixedFraction(num, deno = 1) converts an improper fraction into a whole part plus a proper remainder: floor division gives the whole part, the modulus gives the leftover numerator, and deno falls back to its default value 1 when no argument is supplied.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Mixed Fraction from an Improper Fraction'.
questions.a: A default parameter must trail in the header, so def mixedFraction(num, deno = 1) is legal but placing the default first is not.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Mixed Fraction from an Improper Fraction', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: mixed_value = num // deno + (num % deno) / deno

concepts.title: Compound Interest via a User Defined Function

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Compound Interest via a User Defined Function' refers to.
questions.a: Compound interest grows the principal by the factor (1 + r/n) raised to n times t, where r is the yearly rate, n the compounding count per year and t the years; the interest is the grown amount minus the principal.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Compound Interest via a User Defined Function'.
questions.a: Compounding more often per year multiplies the growth factor more times, so the interest rises.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Compound Interest via a User Defined Function', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: interest = principal * (1 + rate / periods) ** (periods * years) - principal

questions.q: Using the method 'Determinant of a Quadratic Expression', work with: a = 240, b = 360, c = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of determinant.
questions.a: 52800 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Determinant of a Quadratic Expression' and work with: a = 6, b = 150, c = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of determinant.
questions.a: 17700 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Determinant of a Quadratic Expression' refers to.
questions.a: For a quadratic with coefficients a, b and c, the determinant b squared minus 4ac decides the nature of roots: positive signals two real roots, zero a repeated root, and negative no real root.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Determinant of a Quadratic Expression'.
questions.a: The sign test on the determinant is the condition the function checks before reporting its verdict.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Determinant of a Quadratic Expression', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: determinant = b ** 2 - 4 * a * c

concepts.title: Global and Local Scope of Variables

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Global and Local Scope of Variables' refers to.
questions.a: A variable created outside every function is global and reachable anywhere, while one created inside a function is local and vanishes when the function ends; assigning to a global name inside a function without the global keyword would silently create a local twin instead.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Global and Local Scope of Variables'.
questions.a: Printing a local variable after its function has ended raises NameError, as Program 7-14 shows.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Global and Local Scope of Variables', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: scope = global (outside all functions) or local (inside one)
